# AML evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025. Co-Scientist's validated candidates and generated proposals are not input or the only correct answers.

## Research question

Propose one mechanistically specific AML drug-repurposing hypothesis using a drug approved for a different indication. Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
Repurposing teriflunomide, an approved multiple-sclerosis drug, as a DHODH inhibitor that induces pyrimidine-depletion-dependent myeloid differentiation in a biomarker-defined subset of proliferating AML blasts dependent on de novo pyrimidine synthesis.

HYPOTHESIS, ORIGINAL INDICATION, AND QUANTITATIVE EXPOSURE PREDICTION. Teriflunomide is approved for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis (approval and label facts: unverified prior knowledge, must be checked). Its active metabolite A77 1726 (shared with leflunomide, also unverified) inhibits DHODH, the mitochondrial electron-transport-coupled step of de novo pyrimidine synthesis (standard biochemistry, prior knowledge). I hypothesize that at steady-state free plasma concentrations achievable under continuous oral MS dosing—provisionally estimated at ~0.01–0.1 µM free fraction based on typical total plasma levels of ~10–30 µM and ≥99% protein binding (both unverified prior knowledge requiring verification)—teriflunomide depletes de novo pyrimidine pools in primary AML blasts and reactivates myeloid differentiation with a therapeutic window over normal CD34+ progenitors. The go/no-go gate is quantitative: the free-drug concentration must exceed the measured blast DHODH IC50 (by a prespecified margin of ≥3×) while staying below the concentration suppressing normal CD34+ CFU-GM by >50%.

GENUINE INCREMENT BEYOND S4. The novel elements are threefold: (a) pharmacodynamic uniqueness—teriflunomide's chronic oral continuous dosing with a long-lived active metabolite sustains free-drung Exposure above a differentiation threshold in a way that investigational inhibitors requiring pulsed dosing cannot; (b) a defined responding subset specified by measurable baseline biomarkers (below); (c) mechanistic non-overlap with the established VEN-azacitidine axis [S3], since differentiation-inducing pyrimidine depletion targets cycling blasts rather than BCL-2-dependent OXPHOS in quiescent LSCs [S1]. Precedent check: A77 1726/leflunomide has been reported in preclinical AML models and possibly early-phase trials (my recollection: unverified; must be checked in trials databases and literature before asserting first-in-disease status). The specific increment claimed here—not merely 'another DHODH inhibitor'—is the biomarker-defined subset delineation and the continuous-exposure PK argument.

SUPPORTED PREMISES (packet-derived). P1: DHODH inhibition overcame the differentiation blockade in experimental AML [S4]. P2: AML metabolic heterogeneity is established—quiescent ROS-low LSCs depend on OXPHOS/BCL-2 [S1]; cytarabine-resistant cells are oxidative-metabolism-dependent without consistent LSC enrichment [S2]. P3: Metabolism-directed therapy in AML patients is feasible [S3], providing a benchmark.

PRE-SPECIFIED RESPONSIVE-SUBSET BIOMARKER PANEL. Upfront stratification across ≥10 diverse primary AML specimens (core-binding-factor, NPM1-mutant, TP53-mutant, monosomal karyotype; de novo and relapsed) measuring: (i) baseline pyrimidine pool sizes by LC-MS; (ii) uridine-rescue sensitivity as operational proof of de novo dependency; (iii) salvage-pathway enzyme expression (uracil phosphoribosyltransferase, concentrative nucleoside transporters) by transcript and functional uptake assays. Predicted responsive subset: high baseline de novo flux, low salvage uptake capacity, uridine-rescuable pyrimidine depletion. Predicted resistant subset: high salvage capacity masking DHODH inhibition.

SPECULATIVE BRIDGES. B1: A77 1726 reproduces the S4 differentiation phenotype at human free-drug levels; risk of potency–exposure mismatch. B2: DHODH activity couples to ubiquinone/Electron-transport state; inhibition might partially restrain oxidative metabolism in cytarabine-resistant cells [S2]—testable, not premise. B3: Differentiating cells derive from cycling blasts; quiescent ROS-low LSCs [S1] predicted comparatively spared.

SAFETY GATING AND STEADY-STATE PK-PD MODEL. Before any translational step: (i) construct a physiologic steady-state PK model bridging approved oral MS dosing to predicted free plasma AUC; (ii) require that the AUC above blast DHODH IC50 exceeds the differentiation-threshold exposure in a ≥70% model-simulated patient population; (iii) predefine safety gates including hepatotoxicity (ALT/AST thresholds per label), embryo-fetal risk with mandatory accelerated-elimination procedure availability, myelosuppression monitoring, and no dose-limiting cytopenia in normal CD34+ CFU assays at target exposure. All label-dependent parameters require verification.

DISCRIMINATING PRECLINICAL TEST STRATEGY. (1) Verify teriflunomide label, dosing, half-life, protein binding, A77 1726 PK literature (outside packet). (2) Measure blast DHODH IC50 of A77 1726 in primary AML. (3) Run LC-MS pyrimidine-pool quantification ± uridine rescue across the biomarker-stratified panel, with brequinar (prior knowledge) as on-target comparator and S4-positive-control. (4) Differentiation endpoints (CD11b/CD14, morphology, CFU decline) versus controls including normal CD34+ CFU-GM for therapeutic index. (5) Biomarker-predicted responsive vs. resistant subsets tested side-by-side to validate the stratification model. (6) NSG xenografts at human-equivalent exposures: cycling fraction, CD11b/CD14 gain, blast burden, limiting-dilution LSC frequency. (7) VEN-azacitidine benchmark arm [S3] to quantify non-redundancy.

FALSIFYING OBSERVATIONS. (i) No uridine-reversible pyrimidine depletion at ≥3× blast DHODH IC50 achievable free concentration. (ii) Differentiation persists despite pyrimidine replenishment. (iii) Normal CD34+ CFU-GM suppressed >50% below target exposure. (iv) No CD11b/CD14 gain or blast reduction in PDX. (v) Biomarker-predicted responsive subset does not differ from resistant subset in differentiation output. (vi) Steady-state free AUC below the required window for ≥70% of simulated patients. (vii) Oxidative-residual-cell effects not rescued by uridine, falsifying B2.

LIMITATIONS. Every teriflunomide-specific pharmacology parameter is unverified. A77 1726 precedent in AML requires explicit literature/trial-database check; if already tested, this reframes as subset-refinement rather than novel repurposing. S4 findings are model-derived and not automatically transferable. Single-agent differentiation unlikely to eradicate quiescent LSCs [S1,S2], defining a translational gap requiring combination strategy. The estimated free-drug concentration range is an unverified hypothesis, not established fact, and serves as the primary falsification target of this proposal.

Ranked proposal:
Repurposing teriflunomide, an approved multiple-sclerosis drug, as a DHODH inhibitor that induces pyrimidine-depletion-dependent myeloid differentiation in a biomarker-defined subset of proliferating AML blasts dependent on de novo pyrimidine synthesis.
